items.titleOriginal: Maybe This Fall Will Be Kind
items.summaryKo: Yayoi Kusama, Sliman Mansour, and Dolly Parton pass away, and a major Pompeii show comes to the US. From a high platform in the Broadway Junction station, I see a forlorn cloud hovering over the rooftops of East Brooklyn. The sky around it is perfectly clear. The next morning, I find it still standing in the same spot, but it’s faded, famished. That’s how bad things have gotten: The loneliness epidemic has now reached the clouds. Espresso in Williamsburg, watermelon juice in Ditmas Park, writing session in Ridgewood,. soccer camp in Bed-Stuy. At a street corner, a mural by @blkopslife shows a hand holding a famous 1964 photo of Malcom X leaning on the shoulder of his tuxedoed friend, Muhammad Ali. It’s in a Black neighborhood that’s been almost completely gentrified. Dolly Parton suddenly dies at 80. She touched the hearts of millions working nine to five. Sliman Mansour dies at 79. He carried the weight of Palestinian pain on his back. I hope he catches a break in the afterlife. And then Yayoi Kusama follows, passing. at 97. She’ll live on for eternity thanks to her Infinity Mirrored Rooms . At lunch, the guy from the falafel place tells me that all humans were created from a single soul. I say that sounds good, but no lettuce for me, please. I fear it more than death these days. I watch clips of China’s humanoid robot olympics and don’t know whether to be amused or frightened. items.titleOriginal: Robert Indiana’s Maine Home Is for Sale, Despite Late Artist’s Intentions to Make It an Art Space
items.summaryKo: “He wanted and expected a museum of some sort on Vinalhaven and that apparently is not in the cards." Robert Indiana’s longtime Maine home, the Star of Hope, has been listed for $1.4 million despite the artist’s plans for it to become a public art space The foundation established by Robert Indiana to preserve his legacy is selling the artist’s longtime home on the Maine island of Vinalhaven, despite instructions in his will that the property. be transformed into an art space open to the public. The Star of Hope Foundation, as the foundation is called, listed this week Indiana’s former home, a rambling 19th-century Odd Fellows lodge known as the Star of Hope, for $1.4 million, according to the New York Times .
